prompt: Tabulated thermodynamic data for a gas refer to its standard state. What is that state?

choices.text: The pure gas, behaving ideally, at 1 bar
The real gas at 1 bar, just as it actually behaves
choices.why: No real gas is perfectly ideal, so the standard state is the gas behaving ideally at 1 bar. Corrections for non-ideality are made from that reference.

choices.text: The pure ideal gas at 1 bar and 298.15 K
choices.why: Values are often tabulated at 298.15 K, but no temperature is part of the definition. The standard state is the pure ideal gas at 1 bar, at whatever temperature is given.

choices.text: The gas behaving ideally at 1 bar, pure or mixed
choices.why: The standard state is the pure gas, with no mixing. A gas mixed with others is not in its standard state.

explanation: Tabulated values for a gas refer to the pure gas (no mixing) behaving as an ideal gas at a pressure of 1 bar. These are called standard state conditions.

prompt: A table of gas data lists values written as S° and G°. What does the ° symbol on them mean?

choices.text: They are values for the standard state
They were measured at 0 °C
choices.why: Here ° is not the degree sign of 0 °C. It marks a standard-state value: the pure gas, behaving ideally, at 1 bar.

choices.text: They are given per degree of temperature
choices.why: S° and G° are not rates per degree. The ° marks values for the standard state, the pure ideal gas at 1 bar.

choices.text: They are for the real gas at 1 bar
choices.why: The standard state uses the gas behaving ideally, not the real gas, at 1 bar. The ° marks values for that standard state.

explanation: The ° symbol marks standard-state values. For a gas, that is the pure gas behaving ideally at 1 bar, at the temperature stated with the table.

prompt: Standard-state values for gases are often tabulated at 298.15 K. Is this temperature part of the definition of the standard state?

choices.text: No, the temperature can vary and is stated separately
Yes, every standard state is at 298.15 K
choices.why: 298.15 K is a common choice, not part of the definition. Values can be tabulated at other temperatures, so the temperature is stated with them.

choices.text: Yes, the standard state is at 273.15 K, or 0 °C
choices.why: 0 °C belongs to other conventions, not to the standard state. The definition fixes only the pure ideal gas at 1 bar; the temperature can vary.

choices.text: No, because standard values do not depend on temperature
choices.why: Standard values do change with temperature, which is why a table must state its temperature. It is just not part of the definition.

explanation: The definition fixes only the pressure, 1 bar, and the state, a pure ideal gas. Values are tabulated at a specific temperature, often 298.15 K, but that temperature can vary and is not part of the definition.

prompt: No real gas behaves perfectly ideally. Why, then, is the standard state of a gas defined as an ideal gas at 1 bar?

choices.text: So non-ideality is corrected the same way for every gas
Because every real gas is exactly ideal at 1 bar
choices.why: Real gases depart from ideal behavior at 1 bar too, though often only slightly. The ideal reference lets those corrections be made consistently.

choices.text: Because ideal-gas values are read straight from experiment
choices.why: No real gas is perfectly ideal, so ideal-gas values are not measured directly. The ideal standard gives one consistent reference from which non-ideality is corrected.

choices.text: So that gases and solids share the same standard state
choices.why: The section is about gases only. The ideal-gas reference makes corrections for non-ideality consistent across all the different gases.

explanation: Using the ideal gas as the reference means corrections for non-ideality can be made consistently for all the different gases. Each real gas is then described by how far it departs from the same kind of ideal standard.

prompt: Air is a mixture of N2, O2 and other gases. Does a standard-state value for N2 describe the N2 in air?

choices.text: No, it describes pure N2, with no mixing
Yes, as long as the air is at a total pressure of 1 bar
choices.why: Even at 1 bar total, the N2 is mixed with other gases. The standard state is the pure gas, with no mixing.

choices.text: Yes, since N2 behaves almost ideally in air
choices.why: Near-ideal behavior does not make a mixture pure. The standard state refers to pure N2, behaving ideally, at 1 bar.

choices.text: No, it describes liquid N2 at its boiling point
choices.why: The standard state of a gas is the gas itself: pure and ideal at 1 bar. It is not the liquid.

explanation: The section defines the standard state of a gas as a pure ideal gas (no mixing) at 1 bar. The N2 in air is mixed with other gases, so standard values refer to pure N2 instead.
